analysis.one_liner: Sets 18-year term limits for Supreme Court justices, with a seat opening every two years.
analysis.headline: The bill to set 18-year terms for Supreme Court justices, introduced by one senator with 5 Democratic cosponsors, was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would limit Supreme Court justices to 18 years of active service instead of lifetime tenure. A new justice would be appointed every two years — during the first and third years after each presidential election — so each president picks roughly two justices per term. The six current justices would step down from active service in order of seniority as new appointments arrive, and retired justices could fill in temporarily if the Court ever dips below nine.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who lives under Supreme Court rulings — which is everyone. Right now, the Court's direction can hinge on the luck of when a justice dies or retires, and a single justice can serve 30 to 40 years, shaping the law for generations. Under this bill, seats would open on a predictable two-year schedule, so the Court's makeup would track presidential elections regularly instead of turning on chance. Future presidents of both parties would get a steady, equal chance to appoint, and no single administration could stack the Court in one lucky term.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public under Supreme Court rulings

how_it_helps.text: Sets an 18-year term of active service for Supreme Court justices, replacing life tenure, and requires a new appointment during the first and third years after each presidential election — so each president appoints roughly two justices per four-year term.

Ends the current justices' lifetime hold on their seats: sitting justices would be retired from regular active service in order of seniority, starting with the longest-serving, as each new justice is sworn in.

Keeps the nine-seat Court fully staffed during transitions: the most recently retired justice would return to serve whenever the Court falls below nine because of a vacancy, disability, or disqualification.

analysis.who_pays: The six sitting justices, who would give up lifetime control of their seats in seniority order as new appointments arrive — Justice Clarence Thomas, the longest-serving, would be first. The political faction that currently benefits from a long-lived Court majority would also lose that advantage as seats turn over on a fixed schedule, and presidents and senators would lose the ability to remake the Court with several appointments in one lucky term.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sitting justices and their political patrons

drawbacks.text: The bill forces the six current justices off the Court in seniority order within a few years, regardless of their performance or wish to stay — an abrupt rewrite of who sits on the bench, which is why critics attacked it as an attempt to remake the Court by legislation.

It changes tenure by ordinary statute rather than constitutional amendment, while Article III of the Constitution gives federal judges their jobs for life 'during good Behaviour,' so the plan would almost certainly face a legal challenge that Congress cannot shorten life tenure this way.

A fixed appointment every two years does not respond to actual circumstances: seats would open on schedule even if the Court's skill mix or caseload argued otherwise, and the bill changes nothing about how the Court operates day to day.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but structural: predictable, evenly spaced appointments would lower the stakes of any single Supreme Court vacancy and stop justices from serving for four decades. The cost falls almost entirely on the current justices and on whichever political side enjoys the present Court's long-lived advantage, which is exactly why the plan was fiercely contested. The most serious weakness is legal — the bill tries to end life tenure by statute, and that would probably end up before the very Court it seeks to change.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on August 2, 2022, joined by five Democratic cosponsors.
That same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee — the standard first step for a court-related bill.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no hearing or markup and the full Senate never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The sitting justices kept their lifetime seats, and the current Court's ideological balance stayed exactly as it was, because the bill never moved an inch beyond a committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sitting justices and the current court balance

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set 18-year Supreme Court terms and phase out the current justices by seniority.

for.name: 5 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no senator from either other caucus did.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed in committee with no action after referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record was a Democrat — one sponsor plus five of 48 Senate Democratic cosponsors — and no Republican ever backed the bill.

industries.note: The bill ends life tenure: current justices would be retired from active service in seniority order as new appointments arrive, and future justices would serve 18 years. Their interest in keeping lifetime seats runs directly against the public's interest in a regularly refreshed, election-accountable Court.

industries.industry: Judicial nomination pipeline and court-focused advocacy groups
industries.note: With a guaranteed vacancy every two years, judicial screenings, nomination fights, and confirmation battles would become a permanent, predictable industry for legal advocacy organizations of every ideology. The public gets a steadier appointment process, but also a permanent state of partisan warfare over every seat.
